newsitem.title: USA: Step-by-step terms of GM Hughes-Raytheon deal.
newsitem.headline: Step-by-step terms of GM Hughes-Raytheon deal.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s sale of its Hughes Aircraft Co. defense unit to Raytheon Co is a complicated stock-and-debt transaction designed to minimize the tax bill for GM while maximizing the value it gets from the deal.
Here is a step-by-step rundown of how the deal will work:

-- Hughes Aircraft will take on about $3.7 billion to $4.7 billion in new debt, which will primarily be injected into the telecommunications and space business that GM is keeping. The amount of debt vs. stock in the deal depends on Raytheon's stock price, and Raytheon said Thursday it expected the debt portion to be $4.4 billion.
-- GM will effect a tax-free spinoff of Hughes Aircraft to holders of GM's Class H and $1-2/3 par value, or automotive, common stocks.

-- Hughes Aircraft will then merge with Raytheon. The combined company will have two classes of stock -- Class A, to be owned by GM Class H and automotive shareholders; and Class B, to be owned by Raytheon shareholders. When the deal is done, GM's shareholders will own 30 percent of the company, and Raytheon's will own 70 percent.

Raytheon values the amount of stock it will contribute to the deal at roughly $5.1 billion, based on the midpoint of a specified range for its share price of $44.42 to $54.29. Raytheon's stock closed at $48.50 on Thursday, up $1.50.
If the share price falls, Raytheon must assume more Hughes debt to keep the deal's value at $9.5 billion.

-- GM will transfer its Delco Electronics business from Hughes to its Delphi Automotive Systems business. The 25 percent interest in Delco earnings now held by Class H shareholders will be reallocated to GM's main automotive stock.

-- GM will recapitalize its Class H stock into a "tracking stock" linked solely to the performance of its space and telecommunications business. Currently, Class H shares track the performance of the Hughes defense, telecommunications and automotive electronics businesses.
GM Vice Chairman Harry Pearce said GM's lawyers were confident that the Internal Revenue Service will approve the tax-free spinoff.
